nodes.title: Load Image  ->  CUSTOMER PHOTO goes here

widgets_values: A photograph of one dog alone, the only subject in the frame. Head and shoulders, facing three-quarters toward the right edge of the frame, eyes looking at the camera. Dense dark fur with clearly visible coat direction across the cheeks and chest, one ear forward and one laid back, mouth closed, calm alert expression. Soft directional light from the upper left with gentle falloff across the muzzle, highlights on the brow and the bridge of the nose. Plain seamless pale grey studio backdrop holding one even tone, the dog filling most of the frame with clear margin on all four sides. Sharp focus on the eyes, natural fur texture, high detail.

A carved wooden relief portrait of this animal in a flat walnut panel. Smooth sculptural modelling shaped with round gouges, the forms full and flowing, never flat chisel facets. The coat reads as grouped flowing masses that follow the direction the fur lies, broad soft ridges rather than individual hairs. The eyes are rounded domes set under a defined brow ridge with a clear rim around each. The nose is one smooth raised form. The ears are broad simple planes. Matte unpolished wood. Soft raking light from the upper left, gentle gradients across the modelled surfaces, a clear shadow beneath the muzzle and inside each ear. Keep the exact head angle, proportions, ear position and eye spacing. The background is the flat uncarved panel surface, one uniform tone, edge to edge.

Keep the animal exactly as it is. Identical breed, identical head angle, identical ear position, identical eye placement and spacing, identical muzzle length and width, identical coat pattern and markings. Change only the lighting and the background. The lighting becomes soft, even and frontal, filling the shadow side of the face so the muzzle, brow and chest are all clearly readable, with no hard shadow edge anywhere and no blown-out highlights. The background becomes one completely flat even pale grey tone across the whole frame, nothing behind the animal and nothing beneath it. The outline stays crisp, hard and unbroken all the way around, every tuft of fur at the edge cleanly separated from the background.

# Create Portrait Relief

Pet and family portrait reliefs from a photograph. **Every stage reads a FILE**, so an approved image is frozen on disk and cannot drift.

## For a real customer job, start at Stage 1
Point **Load Image** at the customer's photo and leave Stage T muted. Stage T only exists to make synthetic test subjects while the pipeline is being tuned.

## The one node that matters
**Load Image** (teal, left) feeds BOTH Stage 1 and Stage 2. Whichever file you point it at is your position in the chain.

## What the tool can actually cut
At 5 mm depth the 1/16" tapered ball has an effective radius of **1.19 mm**, not 0.79 mm, because the taper flares. The narrowest feature it can cut is about **2.4 mm wide**. On an 8x10 panel:

- eye ~25 mm, iris ~12 mm - comfortable
- nostril and lip line ~3 mm - borderline, keep them as soft grooves
- whiskers, eyelashes, individual hairs - **impossible**

This is why Stage 2 asks for "grouped flowing masses that follow the direction the fur lies" instead of hair detail. Fur that survives machining is fur that was already grouped in the image. Asking the model for fine hair produces detail the cutter turns into mush.

## STAGE T - test subject  (active)
Generates a synthetic pet photo to develop against. Deliberately a moderate-difficulty case: dark fur, side light, visible coat direction.

## STAGE 1 - normalize  (muted)  <- the risky one
Flattens the lighting and the background. **This is the stage that can quietly ruin a commission.** Compare the preview against the original before you approve it - check eye spacing, muzzle length and ear position specifically. A relit photo that is 5% wrong in the muzzle reads as "that isn't my dog" and no amount of good machining fixes it.

A photo with a hard shadow across the face cannot be rescued downstream. We learned that on the raven: a cast shadow measured luminance 34 against the subject's 10-21, and no threshold separates those. Fix it here or reshoot.

## STAGE 2 - sculpted relief  (muted)
Rounded gouge-cut forms, not the flat chisel planes the raven used. Portraits want modelling, not tool marks.

## STAGE 3 - depth map  (muted)
Depth Anything 3. It is noticeably better on faces and animals than on birds - this stage should need less correction than it did for the raven.

## STAGE 4 - silhouette  (muted)
Tune **THRESHOLD** until the animal is solid white on solid black. Ear tips and chest fur are where it breaks.

## Then what
The height field, mesh and STL are built in **Python**, not here. This workflow hands off two files: the **Stage 3 depth map** and the **Stage 4 silhouette**.
